title: Wavelength-Dependent Modulation of Brain Responses to a Working Memory Task by Daytime Light Exposure
research_question: Does the spectral quality (blue vs. green monochromatic light) of short daytime light exposure differentially modulate nonvisual brain activity related to a complex cognitive task (auditory working memory) in humans?

participants.description: Healthy, young subjects (10 females; age: 18-29, median: 23; BMI: 18.7-29.7, median: 22.85). Nonsmokers, moderate caffeine/alcohol consumers, not on medication. No medical, traumatic, psychiatric, or sleep disorders. No color blindness. No night shifts or travel across time zones in last year/2 months. Not extreme morning/evening types. Right-handed.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Short (18 min) daytime exposure to blue (470 nm) or green (550 nm) monochromatic light. Photon density was identical for both: 3 × 10^13 photons/cm²/s. Only one eye was exposed, through a 4 x 5.5 cm frame placed 3-4 cm away from the eye. Order of blue/green light was counterbalanced.

mechanisms: Melanopsin-expressing light-sensitive ganglion cells, maximally sensitive to blue light (470-480 nm), mediate nonvisual brain responses.

Transmission of irradiance signals to hypothalamic nuclei (SCN) and nonhypothalamic structures (e.g., superior colliculi, lateral geniculate nuclei, medial amygdala) by melanopsin-expressing ganglion cells.
Indirect projections from the SCN to cholinergic, orexin, and aminergic cell groups involved in arousal regulation in the forebrain and brainstem.
Direct projections of melanopsin retinal ganglion cells to the lateral geniculate of the thalamus.
Thalamus and anterior insula are key structures mediating the effects of light on brain activity related to cognitive functions.
The swift dynamics of observed effects are likely related to the low dose of light administered.
The effects are independent of behavioral modifications (alertness, performance) and not mediated by the classical visual system (occipital cortex activity was unchanged).
implementation_implications: Future research should establish the optimal light regime (wavelength, duration, photon density, and light history) required to efficiently enhance human cognition during daytime, especially for demanding tasks (e.g., education, military personnel, healthcare professional, police, spaceship crew, and plane crews).

tables.description: Comparison of brain region responses to blue and green light exposure (MNI coordinates) for two interactions: (blue > green) by session (2 > 1) and (blue > green) by session (2 > 3).

limitations: The study design, while consistent with melanopsin system involvement, could not assess the specific contribution of each photoreceptor (cones, rods, melanopsin-expressing ganglion cells).
Current knowledge about the effects of green light exposures is limited, leading to speculative interpretations of observed deactivations.
Pupil size was not assessed, though arguments are made that it would not explain blue light superiority.
